title: Algorithmic threshold for the symmetric binary perceptron
formal:
Does the Gaussian symmetric binary perceptron's polynomial-time search threshold satisfy
\[\alpha_{\mathrm{alg}}(\kappa)=\widetilde\Theta(\kappa^2)\qquad\text{as }\kappa\downarrow0?\]
Precisely, are there constants \(C\ge1\), an integer \(a\ge0\), and \(\kappa_0\in(0,1/2]\) such that for every rational \(\kappa\in(0,\kappa_0]\),
\[\frac{\kappa^2}{C(\log(1/\kappa))^a}\ \le\ \alpha_{\mathrm{alg}}(\kappa)\ \le\ C\kappa^2(\log(1/\kappa))^a?\]
For fixed margin \(\kappa>0\) and density \(\alpha>0\), an instance is an \(\lfloor\alpha n\rfloor\)-by-\(n\) matrix \(G\) with independent standard Gaussian entries. A successful search returns \(\sigma\in\{-1,1\}^n\) with
\[\max_{1\le i\le\lfloor\alpha n\rfloor}\left|\sum_{j=1}^{n}G_{ij}\sigma_j\right|\le\kappa\sqrt n.\]
The threshold is the supremum of fixed rational densities at which a uniform polynomial-time algorithm succeeds with probability tending to one as \(n\to\infty\), in the real-arithmetic model specified below.

The polylogarithmic tolerance restores the tilde lost in the imported excerpt. To make the source's informal efficient-algorithm class definite on exact Gaussian inputs, this card explicitly selects rational-constant randomized real-arithmetic computation. It does not assert equivalence with every discretized or machine-specific version of the conjecture.

why: The symmetric binary perceptron is a basic random constraint model in which many solutions can exist while known algorithms reach much smaller densities. Locating the small-margin search scale tests whether the observed computational obstruction captures all efficient algorithms or only particular algorithm families. Its links to discrepancy, random solution geometry and worst-case lattice hardness make the threshold a substantial average-case complexity question.

The explicit real-arithmetic convention resolves a specification omitted in the source; no equivalence with every finite-precision formulation is asserted. The checked later works do not establish the unconditional full-class statement here. A bounded search found no matching proof or refutation; source-open records these limits rather than certifying all cited preprint arguments.

importance.reason: A fundamental statistical-versus-computational threshold question for a canonical random constraint model, connected to discrepancy algorithms, solution geometry and worst-case lattice hardness; its scope concerns all efficient algorithms rather than a single construction.
importance.basis: Individual model, motivation and primary-source review of the FOCS conjecture and later lattice reductions.

sentences: The symmetric binary perceptron seeks a sign vector satisfying many random Gaussian two-sided constraints.
The conjecture places the efficient-search density at the scale of the squared margin, allowing fixed powers of its reciprocal logarithm.
The card defines a supremum over uniform polynomial-time algorithms and states its exact real-arithmetic convention.
The input dimension tends to infinity at each fixed margin and density before the margin approaches zero.
Stable-algorithm barriers, a sign-matrix algorithm and conditional lattice reductions each have limits that prevent treating them as a full resolution.

definitions:
The dimension \(n\) ranges over positive integers. Margin \(\kappa\) and density \(\alpha\) are positive rational constants held fixed while \(n\) tends to infinity; write \(M=\lfloor\alpha n\rfloor\). The \(Mn\) entries of \(G\in\mathbb R^{M\times n}\) are mutually independent with probability density \((2\pi)^{-1/2}\exp(-t^2/2)\) on \(\mathbb R\). A feasible output is a full vector of \(n\) signs satisfying every displayed two-sided constraint. When \(M=0\), every sign vector is feasible. A failure symbol, a malformed vector or an infeasible vector counts as failure. No conditioning on satisfiability or planting of a hidden solution is performed.

The normalization is by \(\sqrt n\), the square root of the number of variables, and the density is constraints divided by variables. The symbol \(\kappa\) denotes the allowed absolute margin. All constraints are symmetric around zero; there is no one-sided inequality in place of the absolute value. This is the Gaussian version, not a matrix of independently uniform signs. For a nonzero row count the maximum is the usual infinity norm; the empty maximum is taken to be zero.

A permitted algorithm has a finite program with rational numerical constants and finite discrete control, real registers with exact arithmetic, and integer registers for array addresses and loop counters. It can read the supplied matrix, copy values, apply addition, subtraction, multiplication and division, and branch on equality or order comparisons. Integer-address arithmetic is addition, subtraction and comparison; addresses used must be valid nonnegative integers. Each such instruction, register access, input access, output instruction and branch costs one operation. There is no floor, bit-extraction operation on a real register, arbitrary function oracle or infinite program-specific real constant. Division by zero must be handled by an explicit branch, not a source of extra computational power.

For internal randomness, the program may request independent fair bits or independent standard Gaussian real samples, each in one operation. These samples are independent of the input matrix and of all prior samples. The algorithm can be deterministic by making no random requests. There must be constants \(D>0\), \(d\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\) such that it halts after at most \(D(n+1)^d\) operations on every real input matrix of the required dimensions and every sequence of random choices, returning either a sign vector or failure. Space and all input inspection count through these operations. The finite program and constants may depend on the fixed rational pair \((\alpha,\kappa)\), but not on \(n\) or on the sampled matrix. No advice string depending on \(n\) is provided. Exact real arithmetic is a declared computational convention; operation count is not a bound on finite-precision bit complexity.

Let \(\mathcal D_\kappa\subseteq\mathbb Q_{>0}\) be the set of densities \(\alpha\) for which such an algorithm \(A\) exists with
\[\lim_{n\to\infty}\Pr_{G,R}\bigl[A(G;R)\text{ returns a feasible sign vector}\bigr]=1.\]
Here the probability is over both the independent Gaussian entries and the algorithm's permitted internal randomness. The convergence need not have a supplied rate. The algorithm must be one uniform program for the full sequence of dimensions at the fixed parameter pair, rather than a different program at every dimension. Define
\[\alpha_{\mathrm{alg}}(\kappa)=\sup\bigl(\mathcal D_\kappa\cup\{0\}\bigr)\in[0,+\infty].\]
The supremum need not be attained; this definition does not assume an algorithm at the threshold or an all-input guarantee. The main conjecture includes a finite upper bound for sufficiently small margins. Showing algorithms whose densities approach a claimed lower endpoint can establish a lower bound on the supremum even if no endpoint algorithm exists.

In the displayed asymptotic claim, \(\log\) is the natural logarithm and \(\kappa\) approaches zero through positive rationals. The constants \(C,a,\kappa_0\) are chosen once before all those margins. The limit in \(n\) defining the threshold is taken first, separately for each fixed pair. No polynomial dependence of the running-time coefficient or exponent on \(1/\kappa\) is imposed. A statement for a shrinking margin \(\kappa(n)\), or for one fixed value such as \(\kappa=1\), is a different quantifier regime.

The two sides have different meanings: the lower side concerns the existence of successful algorithms at enough densities; the upper side bounds the success densities of every permitted polynomial-time algorithm. A geometric obstruction proved only for algorithms satisfying an additional stability property is not an upper bound for this unrestricted class. Failure to achieve success tending to one does not require success to tend to zero; there may be nonvanishing success or different subsequential behavior.
answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof or refutation of the displayed two-sided polylogarithmic envelope for the defined threshold. A positive answer must establish both inequalities with one set of fixed constants in the declared computational, input-distribution and order-of-limits conventions. A refutation must exclude every permitted choice of those constants, rather than only a selected logarithmic exponent or the stronger claim with no logarithmic loss. Bounds restricted to stable algorithms, experiments, existence of solutions without efficient search, or a result conditional on an unproved lattice hardness assumption do not alone settle the statement. The benchmark target is the asymptotic conjecture, so the numerical 1/100 tolerance does not replace its logarithmic-factor precision.

context_blocks.text: The source conjectures a \(\widetilde\Theta(\kappa^2)\) scale. The logarithmic allowance is part of that conjecture, while the separate question of removing a logarithmic factor and the sharper overlap-threshold prediction are not added to this card’s acceptance criterion.

The full source gives the \(\Theta(\kappa^2)\) algorithmic benchmark via Bansal–Spencer for Rademacher entries and expressly describes transfer of the same guarantee to Gaussian entries as expected. This distribution qualification is preserved; the card does not cite that corollary as a proved Gaussian lower bound.

The source’s geometric obstruction rules out classes of stable algorithms. A bound for a specified stable class is evidence for the conjecture, while a proof of the upper inequality must cover every program allowed here.

Vafa and Vaikuntanathan give worst-case lattice reductions for a margin specified as a function of the inverse aspect ratio. Their stronger logarithmic-scale hardness conclusion uses a stronger lattice assumption. These are conditional results with their own algorithm and parameter conventions; they do not by themselves prove this unconditional fixed-margin real-arithmetic threshold statement.

The January 2026 preprint proposes parametric threshold predictions and reports practical performance of an algorithm. Its abstract does not state a universal lower bound excluding every polynomial-time search algorithm in the model above.
